Prayer, fasting & parish life

Learning to live Orthodox

Becoming Orthodox is not simply learning information about the Church. It is gradually learning a way of life — and it is learned at the pace a person can actually keep, which is why a prayer rule and a fast are set with a priest rather than read off a page.

Should I buy a prayer book?

The parish bookstore stocks them. Which one, and what to pray from it, is worth asking Fr. John.

The parish bookstore is open every Sunday after the Divine Liturgy and stocks prayer books, along with icons, prayer ropes, incense, crosses and candles.

Which prayer book, and what to actually pray from it while you are a catechumen, is the sort of thing to settle with Fr. John rather than to decide off a shelf.

What if I have medical, pregnancy, age or other dietary concerns?

Talk to Fr. John. Fasting is never meant to damage anyone's health, and this is exactly the kind of thing he adjusts.

This is a question to bring to Fr. John directly, before you change anything about how you eat. Health, pregnancy, age, medication and other circumstances are ordinary reasons for the fast to be adjusted, and adjusting it is his to do.

Nothing on this page — or anywhere else on the internet — should be treated as the answer for your own situation.

Can I receive Holy Communion?

Not yet. Holy Communion is received by Orthodox Christians who are properly prepared — which is what you are preparing for.

Holy Communion is received by Orthodox Christians who are properly prepared to receive the Eucharist. Until you are received into the Church, you do not come to the chalice — and that is not a judgement on you, it is the thing the whole catechumenate is pointed towards.

When your first Communion will be is part of your reception, and Fr. John will tell you.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I receive antidoron?

Yes. Antidoron is blessed bread that anyone present may receive, including those who are not Orthodox.

Antidoron is blessed bread that anyone may receive, including visitors who are not Orthodox. It is normally given by the priest after the Divine Liturgy concludes, as people leave for the hall — so you will pass him on your way out, and you are welcome to take a piece.

It is not Holy Communion. It is bread that has been blessed, given as a sign of the shared life of the parish.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I light candles?

Yes. A candle is a small offering made with a prayer, and you are welcome to light one.

A candle is a small offering made with a prayer — for someone you love, for someone who has died, or for yourself. The flame is also an image: Christ is the Light of the world, and a lit candle is one of the Church's oldest ways of saying so.

You are welcome to light one when you come. You are equally welcome not to.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I venerate icons?

Yes. Venerating an icon is something like kissing a photograph of someone you love.

Orthodox Christians venerate icons; we do not worship them. Worship belongs to God alone, and the honour given to an icon passes to the person shown in it, not to the wood and paint.

Nobody is watching to see whether you do it, or checking that you do it correctly. Follow the person in front of you, or simply stand and pray.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I make the sign of the Cross?

Yes — it is prayer made with the body, not a gesture that has to be got right.

The thumb and first two fingers are joined to confess the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit — three, and one. The remaining two fingers are folded to the palm, confessing that Christ is both God and man.

It is prayer made with the body, not a gesture that has to be got right, and nobody is expected to join in before they are ready.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I participate in parish life before I am Orthodox?

In most of it, yes. Come to the services, stay for coffee hour, and get to know people.

Most of the life of the parish is open to you now: the services, coffee hour, the festival, the classes and the ordinary work of keeping a church going. Coming to those things is a good deal of what the catechumenate is.

The sacraments are the part that waits, and a few roles are for Orthodox Christians. Where a particular thing sits, ask Fr. John.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can I attend coffee hour?

Yes, and please do. It is where most people actually meet the parish.

Our Sunday doesn't end when the service does. After the Divine Liturgy we gather in the parish hall for coffee hour — a shared, potluck-style meal, and an old Christian habit of sitting down to eat together after worship.

You do not need to know anyone to come in, and you do not need to explain yourself at the door.

Can I volunteer?

There is plenty that anyone can help with. What a particular ministry needs is worth asking about first.

The parish is kept going by people who help: coffee hour, the festival, the hall, the grounds, the office. Much of that is open to anyone willing.

Some things do assume that the person doing them has been received into the Church, and a few of the sign-ups the site describes do not exist yet. Ask Fr. John or the ministry's own people before you commit to something.

Answer last reviewed 13 August 2026

Can my children participate?

Children are welcome at everything. Whether a child who is not yet Orthodox joins a Sunday School class has not been settled — please ask.

Children are welcome in the church and in the hall, noise and all, and no visiting family has ever been asked to keep a child quiet here.

During the school year, parish children attending Sunday School leave for class after Holy Communion has been served and stay in class until coffee hour begins. Whether a visiting child may join a class that same day has not been settled — if you are visiting with children, please ask a greeter when you arrive and they will help you.
